title: Simple harmonic motion
summary: Learn about the restoring force, oscillation graphs, pendulums and energy.
cards.0.p: When you pull an object a distance x from equilibrium, a spring pulls it back with a force F = −k·x. This force always points toward equilibrium. Motion under such a force is called simple harmonic motion (SHM).
cards.0.key: The minus sign says the force points toward equilibrium. This force is called the restoring force.
cards.1.p: The distance from equilibrium to an end is the amplitude (A). The time for one full back-and-forth trip is the period (T), and the number of oscillations per second is the frequency: f = 1/T. The angular frequency is ω = 2πf.
cards.1.key: Going from −A to +A takes T/2, and going from equilibrium to an end takes T/4.
cards.1.once.soru: A swing makes one full back-and-forth trip in 4 seconds. What is its frequency?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: f = 1/T = 1/4 = 0.25 Hz. So the object makes a quarter of an oscillation each second.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: 4 is the period. Frequency is the inverse of the period.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: For 2 oscillations per second the period would have to be 0.5 s.
cards.2.p: The shadow of a point moving uniformly around a circle, cast on a diameter, does SHM between −A and +A. The period of the SHM equals the time for one turn, and ω equals the angular speed.
cards.2.key: All the SHM formulas come from the projection of uniform circular motion.
cards.2.once.soru: You follow one cabin of a Ferris wheel by its shadow on the ground. How does the shadow move?
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: The shadow shows only the horizontal position, and it goes back and forth between two ends.
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: The shadow falls on the ground and stays on a straight line.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: As the cabin turns, the position of the shadow changes.
cards.3.p: If the object is at +A at t = 0, then x = A·cos(ωt). It passes equilibrium at T/4, reaches −A at T/2, and is back at the start at T. The slope of the graph is the velocity.
cards.3.key: If it starts from equilibrium in the + direction, you write x = A·sin(ωt). At the peaks and troughs the slope, and so the velocity, is zero.
cards.4.p: The speed is |v| = ω√(A² − x²). At equilibrium (x = 0) the speed is greatest: vmax = ωA. At the ends (x = ±A) the object stops for an instant.
cards.4.key: At x = A/2 the speed is not half the maximum speed. It is about 87% of it.
cards.4.once.soru: Where is an oscillating object fastest?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: The force keeps speeding the object up all the way from the end to equilibrium. So the speed is greatest at equilibrium.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: At the ends the object stops for an instant and turns back.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: The speed changes all the time.
cards.5.p: From Newton's law, ma = −kx, which gives a = −ω²x (ω² = k/m). The acceleration always points toward equilibrium. It is greatest at the ends (ω²A) and zero at equilibrium.
cards.5.key: At equilibrium the force is zero, but the object does not stop. Its speed is greatest right there.
cards.5.once.soru: When the object stops for an instant at an end, what is its acceleration?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: At the end the displacement is greatest, so the force and the acceleration are greatest too.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: What is zero at the end is the velocity, not the acceleration. The object turns back right away.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: Acceleration is proportional to displacement. So it is greatest at the end.
cards.6.h: The phase of position, velocity and acceleration
cards.6.p: Position, velocity and acceleration oscillate with the same period. The acceleration graph is the position graph with the opposite sign. Velocity is shifted by T/4 from position. So when x is greatest, the velocity is zero.
cards.6.key: When x = 0 the speed is greatest. In a graph question, look at the x graph first. a is the same graph with the opposite sign, and v is its slope.
cards.6.once.soru: When the position is +A, which way does the acceleration point?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: a = −ω²x. When x is positive the acceleration is negative, so it points toward equilibrium.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: The acceleration always points toward equilibrium.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: The acceleration is greatest at the end.
cards.7.h: The period of a mass on a spring
cards.7.p: The period of a mass on a spring is T = 2π√(m/k). A larger mass makes the period longer, and a stiffer spring makes it shorter. The period does not depend on the amplitude. It stays the same if the spring hangs vertically or is on another planet.
cards.7.key: The period of a mass on a spring depends neither on the amplitude nor on g.
cards.7.etk.soru: Change the mass, the spring constant and the amplitude. Does the amplitude change the period?
cards.8.h: Springs in series and in parallel
cards.8.p: Parallel springs share the load: k<sub>eq</sub> = k<sub>1</sub> + k<sub>2</sub>. In series the extensions add up and the system gets softer: 1/k<sub>eq</sub> = 1/k<sub>1</sub> + 1/k<sub>2</sub>.
cards.8.key: Two identical springs give 2k in parallel and k/2 in series. If you cut a spring in half, each half has a constant of 2k.
cards.8.once.soru: You connect two identical springs side by side (in parallel) and hang the same mass. How does the system compare with a single spring?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: The load is shared by the two springs, and each stretches half as much. So the equivalent constant is 2k.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: Softening happens in a series connection.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: Two springs together pull with a larger force.
cards.9.p: A pendulum swinging through small angles does SHM, and its period is T = 2π√(L/g). The period does not depend on the mass. A longer string makes the period longer, and a larger g makes it shorter.
cards.9.key: The angle should be below about 10°. For L = 1 m and g = 9.8 m/s², T is about 2 s.
cards.10.h: In an elevator and on another planet
cards.10.p: For a pendulum, you use the effective acceleration g' in place of g. If the elevator accelerates upward, g' = g + a, and if it accelerates downward, g' = g − a. In free fall there is no oscillation.
cards.10.svg#12: In an elevator at constant speed g' = g: T is unchanged.
cards.10.svg#13: On the Moon g ≈ 1.6 m/s² → T is about 2.5 times longer.
cards.10.key: What matters is the direction of the acceleration, not of the velocity. In an elevator moving at constant speed the period does not change.
cards.11.p: Without friction the total energy is constant: E = ½kA². At position x the potential energy is Ep = ½kx². At the ends all the energy is potential, and at equilibrium it is all kinetic.
cards.11.key: At x = A/√2 the kinetic and potential energies are equal. If the amplitude doubles, the energy becomes 4 times larger.
cards.12.p: Friction turns the energy into heat, and the amplitude shrinks. This is called damped oscillation. If you push the system regularly at its own natural frequency, the amplitude grows very large. This is called resonance.
cards.12.key: For resonance, the frequency of the outside push must equal the natural frequency. Pushing a swing at the right moments is an example.
cards.13.p:
• The restoring force is F = −kx, and it points toward equilibrium.
• The speed is greatest at equilibrium (ωA), and the acceleration at the ends (ω²A).
• The periods are 2π√(m/k) and 2π√(L/g), and they do not depend on the amplitude.
• For parallel springs k adds up, and for series springs 1/k adds up.
• The total energy is E = ½kA².
quiz.0.q: An object in simple harmonic motion has an amplitude of 0.1 m and an angular frequency of 10 rad/s. What is its speed, in m/s, 0.06 m from the equilibrium point?
quiz.1.q: In a mass-spring system, where is each quantity greatest? Put each one in the right group.
quiz.1.e: At equilibrium x = 0. There the speed is greatest, at ωA, and all the energy is kinetic. At the ends |x| = A, so the force (kx), the acceleration (ω²A) and the potential energy (½kA²) are greatest.
quiz.2.q: In a mass-spring system, what does each change do to the period? Match them.
quiz.2.ciftler.1.0: The spring constant becomes 4 times larger
quiz.2.ciftler.3.0: An identical second spring is added in series
quiz.2.e: T = 2π√(m/k). When m becomes 4 times larger, T doubles, and when k becomes 4 times larger, T is cut in half. The amplitude does not affect the period. In series k<sub>eq</sub> = k/2, so T is multiplied by √2.
quiz.3.q: A simple pendulum and a mass on a spring oscillate in an elevator that accelerates upward. How do their periods change compared with an elevator at rest?
quiz.3.o.1: The pendulum's gets shorter, the spring's does not change
quiz.3.o.2: The pendulum's gets longer, the spring's does not change
quiz.3.e: If the acceleration is upward, the effective gravity for the pendulum is g' = g + a, which is larger. So T = 2π√(L/g') gets shorter. For the mass on a spring, T = 2π√(m/k) does not contain g and does not change.
quiz.3.y.0: The period of a mass on a spring is T = 2π√(m/k). It does not depend on g, so it does not depend on the acceleration of the elevator.
quiz.3.y.2: With upward acceleration g' = g + a. When g' is larger, the period of the pendulum gets shorter, not longer.
quiz.3.y.3: For a simple pendulum T = 2π√(L/g'), so the period depends on the effective gravity. In an accelerating elevator g' changes.
A:ozet: Pull the spring and see the restoring force. Watch the oscillation, read the position-time graph and set the period. Take a pendulum to the Moon, find how the energy is shared, and catch resonance with a swing.
A:adimlar.0.metin: A spring pulls an object that is a distance x from equilibrium back with a force F = −k · x. Here k = 50 N/m. Move the object to a place where the spring pulls it to the left with 5 N.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: For x = +0.1 m, F = −50 · 0.1 = −5 N. The object is to the right of equilibrium, and the force points left. The spring always pulls the object toward equilibrium.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.ipucu: For the force to point left, the object must be to the right of equilibrium. 5 / 50 = 0.1 m.
A:adimlar.1.baslik: What happens when you let go?
A:adimlar.1.metin: You pull the object 10 cm and let go, and there is no friction. The red arrow will show the acceleration and the green arrow the velocity.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: At equilibrium the force is zero, but the object is at its fastest at that moment. So its speed carries it past equilibrium.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: It goes a little past equilibrium and stops
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: That is damped oscillation. In damped oscillation friction turns the energy into heat, but here there is no friction.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: It goes back and forth between two ends
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: At equilibrium the speed is greatest and the acceleration is zero. At the ends it is the other way around. There is no friction, so the amplitude stays 10 cm.
A:adimlar.2.metin: An object on a vertical spring was released from +A at t = 0. The period is T = 2 s, and the graph is the curve x = A·cos(ωt). Slide the time and find the moment the object first reaches −A.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: The object reaches −A at T/2 = 1 s. It passes equilibrium at T/4 = 0.5 s and is back at the start at T = 2 s.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.ipucu: One full back-and-forth trip takes T. Reaching −A takes half of that.
A:adimlar.3.metin: The object oscillates on the end of the spring without friction, and the position-time graph runs below it. When you change the spring constant, the mass and the amplitude, the oscillation changes right away. Find the following for yourself.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.0.yazi: With k = 40 N/m and 1 kg, set the amplitude to 10, then to 20 cm. Does the period change?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.0.tamam: The period stays 0.99 s. When the amplitude doubles, the object travels twice as far but also twice as fast. So the period does not depend on the amplitude.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.1.yazi: Find a way to double the period (≈ 2 s).
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.1.tamam: The relation T = 2π√(m/k) contains a square root. So to double the period you must make the mass 4 times larger or cut k to one quarter.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.2.yazi: Now bring the period down to 0.5 s.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.2.tamam: You need a light mass and a stiff spring. For m = 0.5 kg and k = 80 N/m, T = 2π√(0.5/80) ≈ 0.5 s. A stiffer spring gives a larger restoring force, and the oscillation speeds up.
A:adimlar.4.metin: This pendulum swings through small angles. Change the length of the string and the mass of the ball, and play it at least twice.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: What does the period of the pendulum depend on?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The period comes out the same with the heavy ball and the light one.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: In the trial where you change only the mass, the period does not change.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The period grows with the square root of the string length. When the string is 4 times longer, the period doubles. The mass does not change the period.
A:adimlar.5.metin: The same 1 m pendulum will swing on Earth and on the Moon. On the Moon g is about 1.6 m/s², one sixth of its value on Earth.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: What is the period of the pendulum on the Moon?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The period of a pendulum depends on g: T = 2π√(L/g).
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The period is inversely proportional to √g, not to g.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: When g drops to one sixth, the period becomes √6 ≈ 2.45 times longer. So the period is about 4.9 s instead of 2 s. That is why a pendulum clock runs slow on the Moon.
A:adimlar.6.metin: The potential energy is ½ · k · x², and the total energy is ½ · k · A². The spring constant is k = 50 N/m and the amplitude is A = 10 cm. Move the object to a place where 75% of the energy is kinetic.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.tamam: At x = A/2 = 5 cm, E<sub>p</sub> = ½ · 50 · 0.05² = 0.0625 J. This is one quarter of the total energy (0.25 J). The other 75% is kinetic. The speed here is about 87% of the maximum speed.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.ipucu: The share of potential energy must be 25%: x²/A² = 1/4.
A:adimlar.7.metin: Push the swing at regular intervals, always in the same direction. Find the push interval that makes the swing grow the most.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.tamam: The swing's own period is 2 s, so its natural frequency is 0.5 Hz. Every push came while the swing was moving the same way, and the amplitude grew. This is called resonance. The frequency of the outside push must equal the natural frequency. Friction limits the amplitude.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.ipucu: The pushes should line up with one full back-and-forth trip of the swing.
A:kapanis.0: The restoring force F = −k·x always points toward equilibrium.
A:kapanis.1: The speed is greatest at equilibrium (ωA). The acceleration is greatest at the ends (ω²A).
A:kapanis.2: For a mass on a spring T = 2π√(m/k), and for a simple pendulum T = 2π√(L/g). The period does not depend on the amplitude.
A:kapanis.3: The period of a pendulum does not depend on the mass, and it gets longer when g gets smaller. The period of a mass on a spring does not depend on g.
A:kapanis.4: The total energy is E = ½kA², and it is constant. At an end all the energy is potential, and at equilibrium it is all kinetic.
